$comment: One rotation procedure per credential flow in docs/security/threat-model.md. The readable half is docs/runbooks/credential-rotation.md; this is the half a machine can compare against the threat model. Held on every build by test-unit/credential-rotation.test.mjs, inside `npm run test:unit` → `check:ci` → `.husky/pre-push`.
$why: SECURITY.md says the worst outcome here is somebody spending an advertiser's budget, and the threat model traces where each credential enters, rests and leaves. Neither said how to TAKE ONE AWAY. Rotation is the one procedure in this repository that would be performed under time pressure and had no rehearsal, no page and no dates — while docs/deploy.md § Known red already owes the triage of eleven secret-scan findings whose stated remedy is 'any real credential means rotation'. A procedure discovered during the incident is a procedure improvised during the incident.
$whatBlocks: The SHAPE, not the dates. A credential the threat model declares and this file does not is a credential nobody can rotate under pressure; an entry naming a `TM-nn` the threat model no longer declares is a procedure for a flow that has moved; a cited path that no longer exists sends the reader nowhere at the worst moment. All three are red. Being UNROTATED is deliberately NOT red — see $dates.
$dates: `lastRotated` and `lastDrilled` are null everywhere on 2026-09-01, and that is the honest state written down rather than left blank: an absent field and a never-exercised procedure read identically, and only one of them is waiting for somebody. They are recorded and REPORTED, never blocking — an expiry that turned master red on a morning nobody chose would be re-dated rather than acted on (docs/adr/0007-gate-rung-discipline.md). Rotating a live credential is a RED action under AGENTS.md § What you may do unattended, so no script here may ever fill these in; the operator does, in the same change as the rotation.
$shapes: Which of the four shapes a credential is determines whether there is a window in which both the old and the new value are live. `re-key` is the one that LOSES DATA if it is treated as an overlap; `tenant-action` is the one where 'rotated' is not a state the operator can reach alone.

shapes.overlap: old and new are both accepted for a window: issue, deploy, verify, then revoke the old at the source.
shapes.hard-cutover: one value at a time. There is a gap and it is visible to users.
shapes.re-key: the value is an encryption KEY. Rotating it means decrypting under the old and re-encrypting under the new, or the ciphertext is orphaned. No migration exists in this repository today.
shapes.tenant-action: the operator revokes; the TENANT reconnects or re-pastes. The operator cannot complete it alone.

credentials.name: AUTH_SECRET
credentials.cost: signs out every session. AND: on a deployment that never set CATALOG_TOKEN_SECRET / WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY, both token-crypto seams fall back to this value, so rotating it orphans every stored connector token and webhook secret, for every tenant, permanently. Nothing warns you — decryptToken returns null for 'wrong key' and 'no token' alike.
credentials.verify: sign in again; then confirm a tenant with a stored connector token still syncs rather than reporting no credentials.

credentials.name: FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT
credentials.cost: every store read and write fails while the old key is revoked and the new one is not yet deployed. Issue the new key in Google Cloud BEFORE deleting the old one, which turns the cutover into an overlap in practice even though the variable holds one value.
credentials.verify: load /app signed in; a project list that renders is the store answering.

credentials.name: CRON_SECRET
credentials.cost: none to a signed-in user. The guard fails CLOSED, so a wrong value stops the six schedules rather than letting them run unauthenticated.
credentials.verify: the next scheduled run of each cron in vercel.json succeeds. This is the cheapest credential here to drill: overlap-shaped, no tenant data, fail-closed.

credentials.name: GEMINI_API_KEY / LEONARDO_API_KEY / OPENROUTER_API_KEY / QWEN_API_KEY
credentials.cost: none while both are live. With NO provider configured at all, every AI operation falls back to its deterministic demo answer — a product property, so a botched rotation degrades rather than errors, which is exactly why it can go unnoticed.
credentials.verify: `npm run llm:drift` (AMBER — it spends money) proves the configured provider answers. A degraded-to-demo deployment passes every offline gate.

credentials.name: GOOGLE_ADS_DEVELOPER_TOKEN
credentials.cost: every tenant's Ads read degrades to sample data — flagged, not silent (the connector's degradation flags).
credentials.verify: a connected tenant's campaign table serves live rows rather than a flagged degradation.

credentials.name: RESEND_API_KEY
credentials.cost: outbound mail stops. Nothing here sends without the operator (`no-outbound-under-operator` is an HONOUR rule with no fence), so the blast radius of a stale key is a queue, not a mis-send.
credentials.verify: the operator sends one drafted message through the review gate.

credentials.name: SKLIK_API_TOKEN
credentials.cost: the deployment-wide Sklik fallback stops resolving; per-user Sklik connections (TM-12) are unaffected. A Sklik 401 has no refresher, so it degrades to sample data immediately rather than retrying.
credentials.verify: a Sklik-sourced project serves live campaigns. Never verify by exercising the WRITE path — SKLIK_WRITES_ENABLED is a red action and stays unset.

credentials.name: CATALOG_TOKEN_SECRET
credentials.cost: every stored warehouse/ERP connector token becomes undecryptable unless it is re-encrypted. SETTING this variable for the first time on a deployment that has been using the AUTH_SECRET fallback is the same event as rotating it.
credentials.verify: an affected tenant's catalog sync runs. The failure looks like 'no token', not like an error.

credentials.name: WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY
credentials.cost: every stored outbound webhook secret becomes undecryptable, so outbound payloads are signed with nothing. .env.example flags this at the variable itself.
credentials.verify: one outbound emission is accepted by its receiver's signature check.

credentials.name: BYOM_KEY_SECRET
credentials.cost: every tenant's stored provider key becomes undecryptable and each user must paste theirs again. This is the one credential path with a sast rule of its own — no route may even mention resolveByomKey.
credentials.verify: a byom-tier user's operation runs against their own provider rather than falling back.

credentials.name: Google OAuth access/refresh token
credentials.cost: the affected users sign in again. A revoked token surfaces as a 401, is retried once with a fresh token, and then degrades to sample data WITH the degradation flagged — asserted by test-unit/fault-injection-ads-sync.test.mjs.
credentials.verify: the user signs in and their campaign table serves live rows.

credentials.name: Sklik account token (per tenant)
credentials.cost: the user pastes a new token; the old ciphertext is overwritten. No operator action can complete this.
credentials.verify: the user's Sklik project serves live campaigns.

credentials.name: Warehouse / ERP connector token (per tenant)
credentials.cost: as TM-12. Note the shared seam: a TM-08 re-key forces this rotation on every tenant at once.

credentials.name: Outbound webhook secret (per tenant)
credentials.cost: the user sets a new secret and updates their receiver. A TM-09 re-key forces this on every tenant at once.
credentials.verify: one emission is accepted by the receiver's signature check.

credentials.name: BYOM provider key (per tenant)
credentials.cost: the user revokes at their own provider and pastes a new key in Settings. The operator cannot read it — getPublicByomConfig is what a settings surface reads.
credentials.verify: the user's next operation runs on their own provider.
